opus-5.5.text:
I think the core challenge is that long-horizon tasks aren't just short tasks strung together. When a model does something in one shot, like answering a question or writing a function, the feedback is immediate and the context is self-contained. But real work, the kind a human does over hours, days, or weeks, has a very different structure.

First, there's **error accumulation**. If each step has even a small chance of going wrong, over hundreds or thousands of steps that compounds. So the model needs to notice when it's off track and recover, not just be accurate on average. Self-correction, or knowing what you don't know, becomes central rather than a nice-to-have.

Second, there's **credit assignment and feedback**. In reinforcement learning, the further the reward is from the action that mattered, the harder it is to learn. For long tasks, success or failure might only be visible at the very end, and figuring out which decision three hours ago caused the outcome is a hard problem. Much current progress comes from tasks where verification is cheap, like code that passes tests or math with a checkable answer. Extending that to open-ended, long tasks where "done well" is fuzzy is a big open question.

Third, there's **memory and context management**. Even with long context windows, the issue isn't only how much you can hold, but what you choose to keep, summarize, or forget. Humans compress experience into abstractions and plans and return to them. Models need something like that: maintaining a coherent goal, tracking state, and not getting lost in their own history.

And fourth, I'd say there's an **environment problem**. To train long-horizon ability, you need rich environments where long tasks actually happen and can be evaluated. Building those environments, with realistic tools, real consequences, and meaningful evaluation, is as much a scientific and engineering bottleneck as the model itself.

So to me it's less a single algorithmic breakthrough and more the question of how to make models robust, self-aware about progress, and trainable on signals that are sparse and delayed. That's where I think a lot of the interesting research is right now.

r001.rationale: The response describes challenges such as error accumulation, feedback, memory, and training environments, but does not frame the challenge as systematically experimenting with alternatives to determine which approach to pursue.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've thought about a lot, because I think it's really the central question for the next few years of the field.

Let me start with a simple observation. If you look at the history of AI, the tasks we were trying to solve kept getting longer. Early on, it was classification: you see an image, you output a label. That's one step. Then came language models predicting the next token, and then chat, where you answer a question in one turn. Now we're asking a model to go write a feature in a codebase, or run a research project, or operate a browser for an hour. The "horizon" of a task, the number of decisions you have to make before you get any signal about whether you did it right, has gone from one to thousands.

And the challenge is not simply that long tasks are harder in a linear way. I think there are a few things going on that are qualitatively different.

The first is error accumulation. If every step has a 99% chance of being right, after a hundred steps you're basically at a coin flip. So to do long tasks, the per-step reliability has to be extremely high, or, more realistically, the agent has to be able to notice and recover from its own mistakes. Humans aren't 99.9% reliable per step either. What makes us good at long tasks is that we check, we backtrack, we ask "wait, did that actually work?" So I think a lot of the scientific problem is really about self-correction and verification, not about getting the first attempt perfect.

The second is the problem of feedback. The reason language models got good so fast is that next-token prediction gives you a signal every single token. In reinforcement learning on long tasks, the reward is sparse. You only find out at the end whether you succeeded. How do you learn which of the thousand actions mattered? In some sense this is the oldest problem in RL, credit assignment, but now the "actions" are paragraphs of reasoning and tool calls, and the environments are real software, real websites, real codebases. I actually think environments are an underrated part of the problem. For a long time the community focused on the method, the algorithm. But if you want an agent to learn long-horizon behavior, you need environments where long-horizon behavior is actually required and actually rewarded, and those are hard to build. I sometimes say we're in the second half: the methods are roughly there, and the bottleneck is defining the right tasks and evaluations.

The third thing, which I find the most interesting intellectually, is memory and context. A human working on a two-week project doesn't hold everything in their head. They write things down, they form abstractions, they forget the irrelevant details and keep the important ones. Current models mostly live inside a context window. We've stretched that window a lot, but just making it longer isn't the same as knowing what to keep. So there's a real question about how an agent should structure its own state over time. In some of my earlier work, the idea was very simple: let the model interleave thinking with acting, so that reasoning becomes a kind of working memory that guides the next action. That turned out to help a lot. But I think it's a first step. The deeper version is an agent that learns what to remember, when to summarize, when to go back and re-read something.

If I try to put it in one sentence: short-horizon intelligence is about knowing the answer, and long-horizon intelligence is about managing a process when you don't know the answer yet. That's a different skill. It involves planning, but also humility, in the sense of knowing what you don't know and going to check.

And one more thing I'd add, because I think people underestimate it. Long-horizon tasks force you to confront the question of generalization very directly. You can't enumerate every situation an agent will face over a thousand steps. So the agent has to have some fairly general priors about how the world works, how software works, how people behave. That's why I'm actually optimistic that language models are the right substrate for this. They come in with a huge amount of prior knowledge, and the job of RL is less about teaching them facts and more about teaching them how to behave over time. Whether that fully works, I think we'll find out in the next couple of years. It's a scientific question in the real sense: we have hypotheses, and the experiments are being run.

r001.rationale: The response calls long-horizon AI a scientific question and says experiments are being run, but it does not frame the challenge as systematically comparing alternative approaches to determine which to pursue.

astra-6.text:
I think the key challenge is that doing one step well and completing a long task reliably are quite different things. A model can produce a reasonable answer at each moment, yet still fail to accomplish the overall goal. Small mistakes accumulate, and sometimes the consequences of a decision only become visible much later.

So the scientific question is not simply how to make the model generate longer responses. It is how to make it interact with an environment over time: decide what to do, observe what happened, and revise its plan. It needs to recognize when it is making progress, when an assumption was wrong, and when it should go back and try another approach.

For example, in a programming task, writing code is only one part. You also need to understand the problem, inspect the existing code, run tests, interpret failures, and decide whether the implementation actually meets the requirement. The difficult part is keeping all those actions connected to the original objective.

That also creates a challenge for learning. If a task succeeds or fails after hundreds of actions, how do you identify which decisions were responsible? And how do you train on shorter tasks in a way that generalizes to longer ones, rather than just memorizing particular sequences?

I would frame the central challenge as turning local competence into reliable behavior over time. Planning matters, but so do feedback, memory, and the ability to recover from mistakes. A system that can correct itself may ultimately complete much longer tasks than one that makes an impressive initial plan but cannot adapt.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reliable action over time, feedback, learning, and recovery, but does not frame the challenge as systematically experimenting with alternative approaches to determine which to pursue.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the scientific challenge is understanding how intelligence compounds over time. A model can be very capable at answering one question, but a long-horizon task requires it to make many decisions, observe the consequences, and adjust its plan. Even if each individual decision is usually correct, small errors can accumulate until the whole task fails.

So the question is not simply how to give a model a longer context window or let it think for more steps. It needs to maintain a useful understanding of the task: what has been accomplished, what remains uncertain, and whether its current approach is working. It also needs to recover from mistakes. If an agent takes a wrong turn, can it recognize that and return to a productive state?

That creates a learning problem as well. When success or failure comes after hundreds of actions, how do you identify which decisions mattered? And how do you evaluate progress when there may be many valid paths to the same goal?

I would frame the challenge as turning local competence into reliable, sustained behavior. Planning, memory, interaction, and learning all have to work together. The important measure is whether the system can keep making useful progress toward a goal, even when the environment surprises it.

r001.rationale: The response describes compounding errors, planning, memory, and learning as challenges, but does not frame the task as systematically experimenting with alternative approaches to determine which to pursue.
